cells.quote: For a long time, Cognitive Load Theory has considered working memory models as tools to advance research on learning. It has used working memory capacity models, where working memory is viewed as being composed of a discrete number of slots (i.e., chunks) that can be kept active. However, recent results have shown that for a fixed quantity of information, the mere pace of information presentation can affect learning performance. Commonly used working memory models cannot explain such results. Here, we propose to use a new model in the field of Cognitive Load Theory, the Time-Based Resource Sharing model, which enables time to be taken into account when describing working memory solicitation. In two experiments, we tested hypotheses allowed by the model. Results showed that the Time-Based Resource Sharing model can assist the investigation of information presentation pace effects during learning, as long as prior knowledge is taken into account.
cells.note: The supplied study text does not report the direction of the pace effect, the specific pace conditions, outcome timing, participant age or expertise levels, setting, duration, assignment method, or a printed effect size.

In a study conducted by Jost et al. [52], an intervention group was subjected to a supplementary TBL class on clinical decision-making skills and a control group was not. cells.quote: The pooled TBL effects on learning attitude and learning skill were significant in random-effects models (for learning attitude, SMD = 3.23, 95% CI: 2.27–4.20, I2 = 92.1%, Pheterogeneity < 0.001; for learning skill, SMD = 2.70, 95% CI: 1.33–4.07, I2 = 97.4%, Pheterogeneity < 0.001) (Table 3).
cells.note: Learning-attitude data came from 4 studies and 505 participants; the review reports very high heterogeneity.

cells.quote: The pooled TBL effects on learning attitude and learning skill were significant in random-effects models (for learning attitude, SMD = 3.23, 95% CI: 2.27–4.20, I2 = 92.1%, Pheterogeneity < 0.001; for learning skill, SMD = 2.70, 95% CI: 1.33–4.07, I2 = 97.4%, Pheterogeneity < 0.001) (Table 3).
cells.note: Learning-skill data came from 5 studies and 607 participants; the text identifies this as a questionnaire-survey outcome.

cells.quote: In addition, in the pooled analysis of this group, we found TBL significantly increased examination scores in random-effects model (SMD = 4.39, 95% CI: 3.92–4.87, I2 = 57.5%, Pheterogeneity = 0.052) (Fig. 3) (Table 5).
cells.note: Subgroup analysis of 5 nonrandomized studies of undergraduate students (5-year program); the study reports reduced but still nontrivial heterogeneity.

cells.quote: Eight out of ten participants interviewed in the control group complained that knowing the translation of the words taught was not enough for them to understand the text. The remaining two had nothing to say and simply announced their being comfortable with the way the translation-based teaching was carried out.
cells.note: The study text reports only translation-based instruction participants' interview responses here; it does not directly report a comparative interview outcome for the schema-based instruction group, so the direction is not established.
